questions.q: What is REST?
options: An architectural style defined by constraints, described by Roy Fielding in his 2000 dissertation
questions.explain: Few public APIs satisfy every constraint strictly.

questions.q: What does statelessness mean for the API server?
options: Every request carries all the information needed, and the server stores no per-client session state between requests
questions.explain: The database can have state; the API server just can't hold per-client session memory.

questions.q: Why does statelessness matter for scaling?
options: Any server instance can handle any request, so no sticky sessions are needed
questions.explain: It makes horizontal scaling and load balancing easy.

questions.q: What does the client-server constraint allow?
options: Rewriting the backend (e.g. swapping Postgres for MongoDB) without touching the client if the API contract stays the same
questions.explain: They are independently evolvable components.

questions.q: Which methods are both safe and idempotent?
questions.explain: PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe.

questions.q: What does idempotent mean?
options: Calling it once has the same effect as calling it many times
questions.explain: DELETE /books/17 five times still ends with book 17 gone, though later responses may be 404.

questions.q: Why is GET /books/17/delete an anti-pattern?
options: It violates safety, so prefetchers, crawlers and back-button caching could trigger deletes
questions.explain: Use DELETE for deletions.

questions.q: Is PATCH guaranteed idempotent by the HTTP spec?
options: No: 'set field X to Y' is idempotent but 'increment X by 1' is not
questions.explain: It depends on the operation.

questions.q: Which URL design is preferred?
questions.explain: URLs identify resources (nouns); the HTTP method carries the action.

questions.q: How should a genuine non-CRUD action be modelled?
options: Either a controlled verb segment like POST /orders/482/cancel, or a sub-resource like POST /password-reset-requests; pick one convention
questions.explain: What to avoid is verbs for standard CRUD.

questions.q: How deep should nesting go?
options: Avoid more than 2–3 levels; give deep children their own filterable top-level collection
questions.explain: For example GET /reviews/9/comments or GET /comments/4.

questions.q: Should collections be singular or plural?
questions.explain: It reads naturally for both the collection and singular forms.

questions.q: What are the four parts of an HTTP message?
options: Start line, headers, a blank line, and an optional body
questions.explain: The blank line tells the parser the headers are done.

questions.q: Are HTTP header names case-sensitive?
questions.explain: Header order mostly doesn't matter either.

questions.q: Which should clients check: the status code or the reason phrase?
options: The numeric status code; the reason phrase is informational only
questions.explain: For example 201 versus 'Created'.

questions.q: What does the request line contain?
options: The method, the path (not the full URL) and the HTTP version
questions.explain: The host is a separate header.

questions.q: What is the rule of thumb for a path parameter?
options: If removing the value would leave you unable to say which resource you mean, it's a path parameter
questions.explain: For example /books/17.

questions.q: Which is the better design?
questions.explain: 17 identifies the resource; it isn't a filter.

questions.q: What are query parameters for?
options: Filtering, sorting, paginating or optional modifiers on a collection
questions.explain: If removing it leaves a meaningful, broader request, it's a query parameter.

questions.q: How should GET /authors/3/books?sort=-published_year&limit=10 be read?
options: Path parameter authorId=3 picks which author's books; sort and limit are query parameters
questions.explain: Most real endpoints use both together.

questions.q: What does `curl -i` do?
options: Prepends the response headers to the output
questions.explain: -v goes further and shows the request curl sent.

questions.q: What does `-w "%{http_code}\n"` help with?
options: Checking success or failure in shell scripts without parsing the body
questions.explain: It prints the status code.

questions.q: How do you send query values safely with curl?
options: -G with --data-urlencode, which encodes values like 'Ursula K. Le Guin'
questions.explain: -G turns the data into a query string.

questions.q: When is curl preferred over httpie?
options: For scripting and CI, since it's preinstalled almost everywhere
questions.explain: httpie reads more like English and pretty-prints JSON; Postman suits saved collections and teams.

questions.q: What does authentication answer versus authorization?
options: Authentication: who is calling; authorization: what they are allowed to do
questions.explain: The lesson expands authorization with OAuth2 in Level 3.

questions.q: Why avoid API keys in query parameters?
options: URLs get logged by proxies, browser history and server logs, leaking the secret
questions.explain: Prefer a header such as X-API-Key.

questions.q: What does a leaked API key mean?
options: It's valid until manually revoked; keys carry no built-in expiry or scoping
questions.explain: Never embed a secret key in client-side JS or a mobile app binary.

questions.q: Why must Bearer tokens only be sent over HTTPS?
options: Whoever holds the token can use it, with no additional proof
questions.explain: Sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>.

questions.q: What are the three ingredients of a good error response?
options: The right HTTP status, a consistent structured body, and a human-readable message
A code, a trace and a hash
A status, a redirect and an ID
A stack trace, a cookie and a log
questions.explain: Generic tooling and monitoring check the status first.

questions.q: Why make error.code a stable machine-readable string?
options: Clients can switch on it without parsing English, and it won't change when the message wording does
questions.explain: For example validation_failed.

questions.q: Why is error.details an array?
options: To report multiple validation failures at once instead of making the client fix and resubmit one at a time
questions.explain: For example both email and age issues in one 422.

questions.q: What is RFC 9457?
options: The IETF Problem Details standard for HTTP APIs, with application/problem+json, obsoleting RFC 7807
questions.explain: It includes fields like type and title.

questions.q: Which change is breaking?
options: Removing a field, renaming a field, changing a field's type, or making validation stricter
questions.explain: Rule of thumb: if unmodified client code could start erroring, it's breaking.

questions.q: What are the pros of URL path versioning (/v1/books/17)?
options: It keeps one URL per resource
Very visible and explicit, and trivial to route versions to different backends
questions.explain: The con: the same resource has two URLs, a pragmatic tradeoff Stripe and GitHub accept.

questions.q: Why does versioning matter at all?
options: You can't change a field's meaning or remove an endpoint when consumers you don't control depend on it
questions.explain: It lets old consumers keep working until they migrate.

questions.q: How does header versioning differ?
options: The version is in the body
The version is in the path
The URL stays the same and the client requests a version through a header like X-API-Version: 2
questions.explain: It keeps the URL as the single stable identifier.

questions.q: How is 'a book on a shelf' modelled in the capstone?
options: As a separate /shelf-items endpoint with IDs
As the nested path /v1/shelves/{shelfId}/books rather than a separate shelf-item ID
questions.explain: It avoids inventing an ID the client must track.

questions.q: What do unauthenticated requests receive?
options: 401 Unauthorized with a structured error body (code 'unauthorized')
questions.explain: All endpoints require a bearer token.

questions.q: What is the deliverable of the capstone?
options: A precise, well-documented API design (spec), not a running server
questions.explain: Exactly as you'd hand it to another engineer to implement.

questions.q: Which URL design points does the capstone highlight?
options: The /v1/ prefix, plural resource names, path parameters identifying resources, and nesting for the relationship
questions.explain: They come from modules 3 and 9.

questions.q: What are the two problems with offset/limit pagination at scale?
options: OFFSET scans and discards rows so it slows as offset grows, and inserts or deletes between requests cause page drift
questions.explain: A client may see an item twice or skip one.

questions.q: How does cursor-based pagination work?
options: The server returns an opaque cursor (often base64 of the last sort key) and the next request asks for items after it, e.g. WHERE id > 60
questions.explain: It's an indexed range query, fast at any depth.

questions.q: What is the main limitation of cursors?
options: You can't jump directly to page 5, only traverse forward or backward
questions.explain: They're also slightly more complex to implement.

questions.q: What is page-number pagination?
options: Offset/limit in disguise: offset = (page - 1) * per_page, with the same tradeoffs
questions.explain: It has a more human-readable query shape.

questions.q: How are multiple filter parameters combined?
questions.explain: One query parameter per filterable field.

questions.q: What does ?sort=-published_date,title mean?
options: Sort by published_date descending, then title ascending as a tiebreaker
questions.explain: Compound sort keys matter for stable pagination.

questions.q: What does ?genre=scifi,fantasy usually mean?
questions.explain: Some APIs repeat the parameter instead; both are common.

questions.q: Why should you pick one convention for range filters?
options: Mixing price_gte on one resource and min_price on another makes an API feel unfinished
questions.explain: Stripe uses created[gte]; suffix operators are also valid.

questions.q: What is HATEOAS?
options: Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State: clients navigate the API by following links returned in responses
questions.explain: It's the most-cited, least-implemented part of Fielding's uniform interface constraint.

questions.q: What does a missing cancel link in an order response tell the client?
options: Cancellation isn't currently allowed, so the client needn't copy 'only pending orders can be cancelled'
questions.explain: The server decides which actions are available.

questions.q: Which are two widely used hypermedia formats?
questions.explain: They standardise where links live in the payload so generic clients can parse them.

questions.q: What do most real-world APIs do?
options: Skip a formal spec and use a plain _links or links object, HAL-ish
questions.explain: The lesson shows a minimal ad-hoc convention.

questions.q: What is OpenAPI?
options: A machine-readable specification (YAML or JSON) describing endpoints, request/response shapes and auth
questions.explain: It was formerly called Swagger.

questions.q: What can tools generate from an OpenAPI document?
options: Interactive docs, client SDKs, server stubs and test suites
questions.explain: The spec becomes a single source of truth instead of drifting hand-written docs.

questions.q: What does $ref: '#/components/schemas/Book' do?
options: Reuses a shared schema defined once under components
questions.explain: Book and NewBook are shared definitions.

questions.q: How is the path parameter {id} declared in the spec?
options: As a parameter with in: path and required: true
questions.explain: Query parameters use in: query.

questions.q: Why is POST risky to retry?
options: It typically creates a new resource, so a retry after a lost response can create duplicates
questions.explain: For example two orders instead of one.

questions.q: Which patch is idempotent?
questions.explain: Applying the delta twice decreases the price by 10.

questions.q: How does the idempotency-key pattern work?
options: The client sends a unique token per logical operation; the server remembers processed keys and returns the original result instead of repeating the side effect
questions.explain: It's used for payments and orders, where duplicates are costly.

questions.q: Which methods are idempotent by definition?
options: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD and OPTIONS
questions.explain: PATCH isn't guaranteed.

questions.q: What is the boundary-burst problem of the fixed window algorithm?
options: A client can send 200 requests in the 2 seconds straddling a boundary, well above 100 per minute
questions.explain: Sliding windows smooth this at the cost of more bookkeeping.

questions.q: How does a token bucket behave?
options: Tokens refill at a steady rate up to a cap, each request uses one; it allows short bursts while enforcing a long-run average
questions.explain: A bucket of 20 with refill 10/s lets 20 requests through instantly, then 10 more after 1 s.

questions.q: What does the leaky bucket do?
options: Processes (or discards) queued requests at a constant rate, trading burst tolerance for steady output
questions.explain: It's common in network traffic shaping.

questions.q: What does RateLimit-Reset: 37 mean?
options: Seconds until the window or bucket resets
questions.explain: GitHub's X-RateLimit-Reset is a Unix timestamp instead.

questions.q: What does Cache-Control: no-cache actually mean?
options: It may be cached but must be revalidated with the server before reuse
questions.explain: It's misleadingly named; no-store means do not cache anywhere.

questions.q: What does the server return to If-None-Match when the ETag is unchanged?
questions.explain: The client keeps using its cached copy, saving the payload transfer.

questions.q: What does private mean in Cache-Control?
options: Only the end client may cache it, not a shared proxy or CDN (typical for per-user data)
questions.explain: public allows any cache.

questions.q: What is an ETag?
options: An opaque fingerprint of a resource's current state, often a content hash
questions.explain: Last-Modified is a coarser, second-level alternative.

questions.q: What does Accept: application/json;q=0.9, application/xml;q=0.5, */*;q=0.1 express?
options: Prefer JSON, XML is an acceptable fallback, anything as a last resort
questions.explain: The server picks the highest-q type it can produce.

questions.q: What should a server return if it can't produce any acceptable format?
questions.explain: Many JSON-only APIs skip strict 406 handling, which is fine if documented.

questions.q: What does 415 Unsupported Media Type signal?
questions.explain: Accept negotiates the response; Content-Type describes the request body.

questions.q: Which header handles language negotiation?
questions.explain: It uses the same mechanism as Accept.

questions.q: Why have bulk endpoints?
options: One request per item costs round trips, overhead and more chances to partially fail
questions.explain: 500 records would mean 500 round trips.

questions.q: What status does a bulk request with mixed outcomes return?
questions.explain: The request as a whole doesn't have one status; check each item.

questions.q: Why is partial success the norm in bulk operations?
options: One bad item shouldn't fail the other 499
questions.explain: The example returns 201, 201 and 422 for the three items.

questions.q: What should each item in a bulk result carry?
options: Its own status and either data or an error
questions.explain: The client then inspects each item.

questions.q: Why does the project use cursor pagination?
options: The collection grows continuously as users add books
questions.explain: The response carries next_cursor and has_more.

questions.q: How are unrecognised sort or filter fields handled?
options: Validated against an allowlist; unknown fields return 400 with invalid_sort_field or invalid_filter_field
questions.explain: The allowlist also protects the database.

questions.q: What is If-Match used for on writes?
options: Optimistic concurrency: the write succeeds only if the ETag still matches
questions.explain: It prevents lost updates.

questions.q: What does a retried POST with the same Idempotency-Key return?
options: The original 201 response, without creating a duplicate book
questions.explain: The server remembers processed keys.

questions.q: What is the point of OAuth2?
options: A third-party app gets a scoped, revocable access token without ever seeing the user's password
questions.explain: It's the framework for how a token gets issued.

questions.q: Why does the Authorization Code flow use two exchanges?
options: The code is exposed in the redirect URL but is single-use and short-lived; the token exchange happens server-to-server with a secret the browser never sees
questions.explain: A leaked code alone is useless without the client secret.

questions.q: What is the state parameter for?
options: A CSRF defense: the client verifies the same random value comes back in the redirect
questions.explain: Without it an attacker could trick a victim into completing an attacker-initiated flow.

questions.q: Who are the four OAuth2 actors?
options: Resource owner, client, authorization server and resource server
questions.explain: PKCE is required for public clients like mobile apps and SPAs.

questions.q: How do webhooks differ from polling?
options: The server pushes an event to a registered URL when something happens, with no wasted polling requests
questions.explain: The cost: the receiver needs a publicly reachable, always-on endpoint.

questions.q: How does a receiver verify a webhook?
options: Recompute an HMAC signature over the raw body with the shared secret and compare
questions.explain: Otherwise anyone who finds the URL could POST fake events.

questions.q: Why use hmac.compare_digest instead of ==?
options: Constant-time comparison avoids leaking information through timing
questions.explain: The handler returns 401 for an invalid signature.

questions.q: What should a webhook receiver do quickly?
options: Respond (e.g. 200) fast and process heavy work separately
questions.explain: Slow responses cause the sender to retry.

questions.q: What is an API gateway?
options: The single entry point in front of services that routes, secures and shapes traffic
questions.explain: Clients don't need to know every backend's address.

questions.q: Why validate tokens once at the gateway?
options: Individual services don't each re-implement JWT verification
questions.explain: It's authentication at the edge.

questions.q: What does TLS termination at the gateway mean?
options: The gateway holds the certificate; internal traffic can run plain HTTP inside a trusted network
questions.explain: It's one of the gateway's jobs.

questions.q: Which of these is a gateway responsibility?
options: Routing, auth, rate limiting, transformation and observability
questions.explain: For example /v1/orders/* goes to orders-service.

questions.q: What problems does GraphQL address compared with REST?
options: Over-fetching, under-fetching (chains of calls) and client-driven response shape
questions.explain: One request returns exactly the fields asked for.

questions.q: Why does GraphQL defeat standard HTTP caching?
options: A single POST /graphql endpoint isn't cacheable by URL, so caching must be rebuilt at the application layer
questions.explain: For example persisted queries and a normalized client cache.

questions.q: Why do GraphQL servers need query complexity analysis?
options: One query can ask for deeply nested, expensive data, unlike a REST endpoint with predictable cost
questions.explain: It prevents abuse.

questions.q: What is the GraphQL schema?
options: A typed definition of the data the client can query, e.g. type User { id: ID! name: String! }
questions.explain: The exclamation mark means non-null.

questions.q: What does the API testing pyramid say?
options: Many fast unit tests at the bottom, then contract and integration tests, with few slow end-to-end tests on top
questions.explain: Most bugs should be caught at the bottom layers.

questions.q: What does an integration test catch that a unit test can't?
options: A wrong status code or JSON shape, or a route that isn't wired up, against a real test DB and the real HTTP layer
questions.explain: It also verifies the row landed in the DB.

questions.q: How does consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) work?
options: The consumer records what it expects; the provider's CI replays that contract before every deploy
questions.explain: It catches breaking changes without needing both full codebases.

questions.q: What is the purpose of end-to-end tests?
options: To catch what only shows up when the whole system runs together
questions.explain: They are few and slow.

questions.q: Which is a non-breaking change?
options: Adding an optional response field or a new endpoint
questions.explain: Well-behaved clients ignore what they don't recognise.

questions.q: What do the Deprecation and Sunset headers do?
options: Let tooling detect deprecated usage and the retirement date without humans reading changelogs
questions.explain: A Link header can point to the migration guide.

questions.q: Why is URL-path versioning the most common?
options: It's visible, cacheable per version and trivial to route at the gateway
questions.explain: Header versioning is harder to test in a browser and easy to forget.

questions.q: How should v1 be retired?
options: Ship v2 alongside, announce with a concrete sunset date, then remove after the runway
questions.explain: Bundle breaking changes into one release rather than drip-feeding.

questions.q: Why generate reference docs from the OpenAPI spec?
options: They stay accurate because they're generated, not hand-written
questions.explain: Guides and tutorials are hand-written.

questions.q: What is a changelog's role?
options: A dated, human-readable list of changes linked to migration guides for breaking changes
questions.explain: It's part of the documentation stack.

questions.q: What does an interactive playground allow?
options: Making a real call from the browser, such as Swagger UI, Redoc or Postman collections
questions.explain: It lowers the barrier to a first request.

questions.q: What is the key doc goal described?
options: Usable by a developer integrating for the first time at 11pm with no one to ask
questions.explain: Guides are task-oriented.

questions.q: What does gRPC use?
options: Compact binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, with services defined in a .proto file
questions.explain: It generates strongly typed client and server code in many languages.

questions.q: Why does gRPC catch contract mismatches earlier than REST/JSON?
options: The .proto file is the single source of truth generated on both sides, so mismatches fail at compile time
questions.explain: With JSON, a malformed body fails at runtime.

questions.q: Why does REST still win for public and browser-facing APIs?
options: Browsers can't natively speak gRPC, REST/JSON is debuggable with curl, and public integrators expect REST
questions.explain: gRPC-Web exists but adds a proxy layer.

questions.q: Where is gRPC the common choice?
questions.explain: Both sides control their codegen pipeline within one company.

questions.q: What are the four golden signals?
questions.explain: Saturation is the leading indicator before latency and errors spike.

questions.q: Why alert on error rate rather than raw error count?
options: 12 errors in 18,432 requests (0.07%) is very different from 12 in 40 (30%)
questions.explain: The rate tells you how bad it is.

questions.q: What does distributed tracing show?
options: How one request fans out across services under a trace_id, revealing e.g. a slow Postgres query in orders-service
questions.explain: Without it, 'the dashboard is slow' is a mystery.

questions.q: Why use structured JSON logs with request_id?
options: They're queryable, and request_id threads through every log line and downstream call for a request
questions.explain: The request_id is generated at the gateway.

questions.q: Which OAuth2 flow does the project use?
questions.explain: The token exchange includes code_verifier.

questions.q: What happens when a token has only books:read and tries POST /v1/books?
questions.explain: The test test_requires_write_scope asserts 403.

questions.q: Where is the OAuth2 token signature validated?
options: Once at the gateway, before the request reaches books-service or webhooks-service
questions.explain: The gateway applies jwt and rate-limiting plugins.

questions.q: How are webhook deliveries made reliable and trustworthy?
options: Signed with the webhook's secret via X-Signature and retried with exponential backoff on failure
questions.explain: The subscriber receives a secret when registering.

questions.q: What does database-per-service mean?
options: Each microservice owns its database and no service reaches into another's tables
questions.explain: orders-service calls users-service's API for a user's name.

questions.q: What is the API composition pattern?
options: A gateway or BFF layer merges data from multiple services into one response
questions.explain: The client sees one endpoint like /v1/orders/42/summary.

questions.q: What is a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)?
options: A layer per client type (mobile, web) shaping responses, such as a lean mobile payload versus a full web one
questions.explain: Different clients need different shapes from the same services.

questions.q: Why does database-per-service make services independently deployable?
options: No one can break another team's queries by changing a table they don't own
questions.explain: It's the key ownership rule.

questions.q: What does BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) mean?
options: Checking that a token is valid but not that this user owns this specific resource
questions.explain: The fix: every lookup filters by the authenticated user as well as the ID.

questions.q: What is the safe way to handle a user-supplied sort parameter?
options: Validate against an allowlist of known-safe columns, and use parameterized queries
questions.explain: ?sort=id;DROP+TABLE+orders is catastrophic when interpolated directly.

questions.q: What is the correct CORS configuration?
options: An explicit origin allowlist (e.g. https://app.example.com) with Vary: Origin, not reflecting any Origin
questions.explain: Reflecting Origin recreates the hole even though browsers reject * with credentials.

questions.q: What happens to a preflight from an origin not on the allowlist?
options: It's rejected, so the browser never sends the real request
questions.explain: The example returns 403 for evil.com.

questions.q: Why does a public product listing with Cache-Control: public, max-age=300 scale well?
options: It's served from the CDN edge for 5 minutes, so the origin never sees most of the traffic
questions.explain: Private per-user caching still hits the origin but skips the database.

questions.q: Why invalidate the Redis cache on write, not just by expiry?
options: So the next read repopulates fresh data instead of serving stale data until the TTL
questions.explain: update_product deletes the key.

questions.q: What does connection pooling solve?
options: Opening a DB connection per request is expensive (TCP handshake, auth); a pool reuses warm connections
questions.explain: Too small a pool makes requests queue; too large overwhelms the database. Size by measurement.

questions.q: Why return 202 Accepted for a long report job?
options: The client gets an immediate response with a job ID, then polls or receives a webhook when it's done
questions.explain: Generating the report might take two minutes.

questions.q: Why is the raw API key shown only once at creation?
options: To hide it from the owner
Only its prefix and metadata are kept retrievable, so a leaked key can be identified and revoked without storing the plaintext
questions.explain: Keys are scoped and revocable independently.

questions.q: What does an sk_test_ key route to?
options: A fully isolated sandbox with fake payment processing and resettable data
A staging server shared with all
questions.explain: The key prefix signals the environment.

questions.q: Why generate SDKs from the OpenAPI spec?
options: Every language binding stays in sync automatically as the spec changes
questions.explain: Hand-maintained SDKs drift out of date.

questions.q: Why publish rate limit headers for public APIs?
options: Third-party developers build automated systems against them and can't just be told by your team
questions.explain: For example X-RateLimit-Limit, Remaining and Reset.

questions.q: What is a design-first review process?
options: Teams submit an OpenAPI spec for review before writing implementation code
questions.explain: Catching inconsistency at spec stage is far cheaper than migrating later.

questions.q: What does the style guide excerpt say about money?
options: Integer cents with a _cents suffix (total_cents: 4250), never a float
questions.explain: Timestamps are ISO 8601 UTC with an _at suffix.

questions.q: What does a written style guide change about reviews?
options: Subjective comments become objective checks against a section, giving faster reviews and less friction
questions.explain: It's the actual standard.

questions.q: Why does governance matter with dozens of teams?
options: Without coordination APIs diverge in pagination, error formats and auth, instead of feeling like one coherent platform
questions.explain: The checklist covers pagination, errors, naming, versioning and scopes.

questions.q: What are the three reasons for multi-region?
options: Latency, availability and regulatory data residency
questions.explain: A Singapore customer on a US-only API pays about 200 ms of network transit.

questions.q: How do active-passive and active-active differ?
options: Active-passive has one region serving with a replicated idle standby; active-active has several serving live traffic at once
questions.explain: Active-active is harder (cross-region consistency) but wastes no capacity.

questions.q: What happens to a region failing health checks?
options: It's automatically removed from DNS/routing so traffic reroutes within seconds
questions.explain: GeoDNS routes customers to their nearest healthy region.

questions.q: What's the hard part of multi-region?
options: The database and data consistency; stateless app servers replicate trivially
questions.explain: There is a trade-off between consistency and write latency.

questions.q: What is the difference between a request and an event?
options: A request says 'do this and tell me what happened'; an event says 'this happened' with no expectation of who reacts
questions.explain: orders-service publishes order.confirmed without knowing its consumers.

questions.q: Why do brokers durably store events?
options: A consumer that's down processes the backlog when back, instead of losing the event as a failed direct HTTP call would
questions.explain: Examples: Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ.

questions.q: Why must consumers be idempotent?
options: Brokers give at-least-once delivery, so the same event may arrive twice
questions.explain: Check processed_events before handling.

questions.q: What does the outbox pattern solve?
options: Losing events on a crash between a DB write and a publish, by writing the event in the same transaction and relaying it separately
questions.explain: Either both commit or neither does.

questions.q: Why record usage metering asynchronously?
options: So metering adds no latency to the actual response
questions.explain: It uses the event-driven pattern from module 7.

questions.q: How does quota exhaustion differ from rate limiting?
options: It's a billing boundary that resets on the billing cycle, and the fix is upgrading a plan rather than waiting 60 seconds
questions.explain: Both can return 429, but the semantics differ.

questions.q: Why offer a real-time usage dashboard?
options: It avoids a customer discovering a huge bill at month end with no warning
questions.explain: It returns calls_used, calls_included and projected overage.

questions.q: What does a developer portal bundle?
options: Sign-up and key generation, docs, usage dashboard, billing and plan upgrades, and support links
questions.explain: It makes a paid API self-service.

questions.q: What is the danger window in a rolling deploy?
options: Old and new code serve traffic simultaneously, so a change incompatible with the previous version breaks requests
questions.explain: It lasts seconds to minutes.

questions.q: What are the three phases of expand-contract?
options: Expand (add the new column and write both), migrate (backfill and switch reads), contract (drop the old column)
questions.explain: Each is an independent, individually safe deploy.

questions.q: Why backfill all rows before switching reads?
options: Otherwise old rows read as null
questions.explain: Switch reads only after every row is backfilled.

questions.q: How does a rolling deployment protect against a bad build?
options: New instances are health-checked before receiving traffic, and a failing one halts the rollout
questions.explain: The load balancer only routes to healthy instances.

questions.q: What is the capstone, OrderFlow?
options: A design exercise: a public, monetized, multi-region order/inventory/payments API at tens of thousands of requests per second
questions.explain: Work through each decision as in a real architecture review and justify it.

questions.q: What is expected of each decision?
options: Be able to justify it, as in an architecture review
questions.explain: It pulls together every module from all four levels.

questions.q: What do the capstone's requirements span?
options: All four levels: REST design, pagination, auth, webhooks, gateways, security, performance, governance, multi-region, events, monetization and zero-downtime releases
questions.explain: The platform is monetized as a paid product.

questions.q: What scale does the brief set?
options: Tens of thousands of requests per second across multiple continents
questions.explain: That scale drives the multi-region and performance choices.

questions.q: A mobile client POSTs /payments, the network times out, and it retries the same request. How should the API prevent a double charge?
options: Make POST idempotent by changing it to GET
Ask the user to wait a minute
Require an Idempotency-Key header; return the stored original result when the key repeats
questions.explain: Verified by simulation: the second call with the same key returns the original result (status 200 versus 201 for a new key) and creates no second record.

questions.q: A client's list request used offset pagination: page 1 returned ids [1, 2, 3]. Before page 2, a new item was inserted at the front. What does page 2 (offset 3) return?
questions.explain: Offsets shift when rows are inserted or deleted. Cursor pagination (WHERE id > last_id) avoids this.

questions.q: A token bucket has capacity 3 and refills 1 token per second. Requests arrive at t = 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2 seconds. Which are allowed (1) or rejected (0)?
questions.explain: The burst of three drains the bucket, the 4th is rejected, then one token returns per second. Verified by simulation.

questions.q: `GET /v1/orders/999` with user A's valid token returns user B's order. Which vulnerability is this, and what is the fix?
options: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA); filter every lookup by the authenticated user as well as the ID
questions.explain: Checking only that a token is valid isn't enough. Returning 404 for others' resources also avoids confirming they exist.

questions.q: A client sends `If-None-Match: "b7e2f9"` and the resource hasn't changed. What does the server return?
questions.explain: The client keeps using its cached copy. If-Match (not If-None-Match) is for optimistic concurrency on writes.

questions.q: A client sends `If-Match: "old-etag"` on a PUT but the resource has changed since. What should the server return?
options: 412 Precondition Failed, so the client doesn't overwrite someone else's change
questions.explain: If-Match gives optimistic concurrency and prevents lost updates.

questions.q: You must rename the `total` column to `total_amount` on a live API with rolling deploys. What is the safe order?
options: Stop the API for the migration window
Expand (add column, write both), migrate (backfill, switch reads), contract (drop the old column), each as a separate deploy
questions.explain: During a rolling deploy old and new code run together, so every step must be compatible with both versions.

questions.q: An endpoint accepts `?sort=` and builds `ORDER BY` from it. Which fix is correct?
options: Validate against an allowlist of known columns (and use parameterised queries elsewhere)
questions.explain: Never interpolate user input into SQL, even for ORDER BY.

questions.q: A public API returns `429 Too Many Requests` with `RateLimit-Reset: 37`. What should a well-behaved client do?
options: Switch to a different API key
Wait about 37 seconds (the time until the window resets) before retrying
questions.explain: RateLimit-Reset here means seconds until the window or bucket resets. A Retry-After header may also be present.

questions.q: A webhook receiver gets a POST with an X-Webhook-Signature header. What is the right verification?
options: Recompute the HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with the shared secret and compare in constant time
Check that the request came from a known IP only
Parse the JSON and trust the event id
Compare the signature with == on the parsed body
questions.explain: Verify the raw bytes. Parsing and re-serialising can change them, and == leaks timing information.

questions.q: A report takes two minutes to generate. Which design is best?
options: POST returns 202 Accepted with a job id; the client polls the job or receives a webhook
Hold the connection open for two minutes
Return 504 and ask the client to retry
questions.explain: Long work belongs in a background job, not in the request.

questions.q: Which change to an existing v1 response is breaking?
options: Renaming a field or changing its type (for example 42 to "42")
Adding a new optional query parameter
questions.explain: Rule of thumb: if unmodified client code could start erroring, it's breaking.

questions.q: Which headers help clients prepare for retiring v1?
options: Deprecation and Sunset (with a Link to the migration guide)
questions.explain: They let tooling detect deprecated usage and the removal date automatically.

questions.q: An orders service needs the customer's name, which lives in another team's database. What is the microservices-correct approach?
options: Add a read-only DB connection to users_db
Call the users service's API (or consume its events); never query its tables
Copy the tables nightly by hand
questions.explain: Database-per-service keeps services independently deployable.

questions.q: After the orders service writes the order row, it crashes before publishing `order.confirmed`. Which pattern avoids lost events?
options: The transactional outbox: write the event row in the same DB transaction and relay it separately
Publish first, then write the row
questions.explain: Both writes commit or neither does; a relay publishes from the outbox.

questions.q: A broker delivers the same event twice after a rebalance. What must the consumer be?
options: Idempotent: it records processed event ids and skips duplicates
questions.explain: Most brokers give at-least-once delivery.

questions.q: A browser app on https://app.example.com calls your API. Which CORS setup is right?
options: Allow that explicit origin (with Vary: Origin), not a reflected or wildcard origin with credentials
questions.explain: Reflecting any origin recreates the hole the same-origin policy is protecting against.

questions.q: Which protocol suits internal service-to-service calls with strong contracts and streaming, and which suits public browser-facing APIs?
questions.explain: Browsers can't natively speak gRPC, and public integrators expect REST.

challenges.title: Cursor pagination
challenges.prompt: Implement list_books(limit, cursor=None) over BOOKS (ids 1..7). The cursor is the base64 (urlsafe) of JSON {"id": last_id}. Return {data: ids, has_more, next_cursor}. Fetch limit+1 rows to know whether more exist. Then page through with limit 3.
challenges.starter:
import base64, json
BOOKS = [{"id": i, "title": f"Book {i}"} for i in range(1, 8)]

def encode_cursor(last_id):
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps({"id": last_id}).encode()).decode()

def decode_cursor(cursor):
    return json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(cursor.encode()))["id"]

def list_books(limit, cursor=None):
    # your code
    pass

p1 = list_books(3)
p2 = list_books(3, p1["next_cursor"])
p3 = list_books(3, p2["next_cursor"])
print(p1["data"], p1["has_more"], decode_cursor(p1["next_cursor"]))
print(p2["data"], p2["has_more"])
print(p3["data"], p3["has_more"], p3["next_cursor"])
challenges.explain: Fetching limit+1 rows tells you whether another page exists without a count query. The cursor encodes the last id, so the next page is WHERE id > last_id, which stays consistent when rows are inserted or deleted. Verified by running the solution: output matches.
